### 1.3. Load the dataset

```{r part1-data}
```

The `NMES1988` dataset contains `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` respondents from the US National Medical Expenditure Survey. The outcome is the number of physician office visits. The predictors are number of chronic conditions, self-perceived health, gender, years of education, and private insurance coverage.

The reference groups are **average** for health, **male** for gender, and **no** for private insurance.

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Distribution of physician office visits."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart counting participants at each observed number of physician office visits."
descriptive_plot
```

The outcome is a count of physician office visits, so it takes whole-number values starting at zero. About `r round(100 * visits_summary$p_zero, 1)`% of participants had no visits. Most people had few visits, but the chart has a long tail to the right, with a few high counts and a maximum of `r visits_summary$max` visits. The variance (`r round(visits_summary$var, 2)`) is much higher than the mean (`r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`), so I’ll check whether the Poisson model can account for that much variation.

## Part 2. Specify competing count models

### 2.1. Why not a linear model?

```{r part2-gaussian}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gaussian-dharma
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the Gaussian model."
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa plot with a residual Q–Q plot and a residuals-versus-predicted plot."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(res_gauss)
```

Both DHARMa plots suggest that the Gaussian model fits the visit counts poorly. In the Q–Q plot, the black points curve away from the red diagonal, so the residuals look different from what we would expect with a good fit. In the right panel, the middle red curve stays below the middle dashed line, suggesting that the model tends to predict too many visits. The outer curves spread farther apart at higher predicted visit counts, and the stars mark observed counts higher than all the simulations for those people. This linear model assumes that the expected count changes by a fixed amount for each extra unit of a numeric predictor. It also assumes bell-shaped errors with the same spread at every prediction and can simulate negative values. The real visit counts are whole numbers starting at zero, with many low counts and a few very high ones.

### 2.2. Specify three nested Poisson models

```{r part2-poisson}
```

| Model | Predictors |
|----|----|
| M0 Null | Intercept only |
| M1 Chronic | Number of chronic conditions |
| M2 Full | Chronic conditions, health, gender, schooling, and private insurance |

### 2.3. Compare the fitted models

```{r part2-anova}
```

```{r part2-table}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-poisson-comparison
poisson_table
```

The comparison of the chronic model with the null model gave χ² = `r sprintf("%.2f", comparison_table$Nested.Chisq.stat[2])` with `r comparison_table$Nested.df[2]` degree of freedom (*p* `r format.pval(comparison_table$Nested.p.value[2], digits = 3, eps = .001)`). The comparison of the full model with the chronic model gave χ² = `r sprintf("%.2f", comparison_table$Nested.Chisq.stat[3])` with `r comparison_table$Nested.df[3]` degrees of freedom (*p* `r format.pval(comparison_table$Nested.p.value[3], digits = 3, eps = .001)`).

The likelihood-ratio tests showed that adding chronic conditions improved the fit over the null model. Adding health, gender, schooling, and insurance improved the fit further. I chose M2 as the Poisson model to carry forward because it had the highest (least negative) log-likelihood, so it fit the observed visit counts best of the three models. M2 also had the lowest AIC and BIC, so it was still preferred after accounting for the extra predictors. I’ll check how well M2 fits the data in Part 3.

## Part 3. Evaluate the Poisson model

### 3.1. Simulate residuals

```{r part3-dharma}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-poisson-dharma
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the full Poisson model."
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa Q–Q and residuals-versus-predicted plots for the full Poisson model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot(res_pois)
```

### 3.2. Test for overdispersion and excess zeros

```{r part3-tests}
```

The dispersion ratio was `r sprintf("%.2f", disp_pois$statistic)` (simulation *p* = `r format.pval(disp_pois$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0)`). The ratio of observed to expected zeros was `r sprintf("%.2f", zi_pois$statistic)` (simulation *p* = `r format.pval(zi_pois$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0)`). A simulation *p*-value displayed as zero means none of the `r res_pois$nSim` simulations was as extreme as the observed result.

### 3.3. Interpret the diagnostics

The Q–Q plot bends away from the diagonal, and residuals pile up near both ends of the right panel. This suggests the Poisson model struggles with very low and very high counts. The dispersion ratio was `r sprintf("%.2f", disp_pois$statistic)`, and there were `r sprintf("%.2f", zi_pois$statistic)` times as many zeros as expected. Poisson assumes the variance equals the mean. With extra variation, its standard errors and *p*-values tend to be too small and its confidence intervals too narrow. I’ll check whether a negative binomial model’s extra spread can account for the zeros before adding a separate model for them.
